items.headline: Warsh's AI speech: three possible futures, and not a word on interest rates
items.caption: The Fed chair laid out good, mixed and bad AI scenarios at a San Francisco forum. He skipped rate hints, weeks before the Dec. 9 decision.

visual.title: Warsh's 3 AI scenarios (not forecasts)
items: 1. Gains shared widely, growth above average, jobs near full
2. Growth rises but automation pushes unemployment up
3. AI payoffs disappoint, stocks fall, a slowdown comes first
Fed role: prepare, not cheer or fight AI

detail: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh opened the Fed's Productivity and Jobs Task Force conference Monday. He called super-intelligent AI a general-purpose technology that could change economic life and make expert answers far cheaper.

He sketched three paths. In one, gains are broadly shared. In another, growth rises but job losses lift unemployment. In the third, the huge AI investment wave fails to pay off, stocks fall and the economy slows before recovering.
He said the Fed should neither push nor block AI, only prepare, and that AI could matter for monetary policy later. He did not discuss rates, even as markets expect a hike on Dec. 9.
money: A Fed chair openly naming an AI bust scenario is a reason to check how much of your portfolio rides on AI stocks.
Scenario 2 means job risk can rise even in a strong economy; a 3-6 month emergency fund is your hedge.
With no rate signal, keep planning for the expected December hike: lock fixed rates on loans and savings CDs where it helps.
risk: These are illustrations, not Fed forecasts; the path could be none of them.

items.headline: Fed's Barr: AI agents moving money on their own could turn bank runs into minutes
items.caption: Fed Governor Michael Barr warned that many AI agents reacting to the same signal could pull deposits at once. He urged strict consent and limits on what agents can do.

visual.title: How fast runs can be
visual.label: Silicon Valley Bank lost about $42 billion in one day in March 2023, with humans clicking.

detail: Speaking in Milan on Monday, Fed Governor Michael Barr said autonomous AI agents could speed up bank runs by moving deposits automatically when they spot yield gaps or stress.

His biggest worry is herd behavior: many agents built on similar models could react to the same signal in seconds. He also said bad actors could feed false information to many systems at once, and that banks already see agents trying actions in accounts without verified consent.
Barr suggested strict authentication, consent tied to each action, and technical limits on agents. He did not propose a new rule.
money: Keep deposits under the $250,000 FDIC limit per bank, per ownership category, so a run doesn't put your cash at risk.
Before giving any AI tool access to your bank account, check what it can do without asking you.
Turn on account alerts so you see any money movement right away.
risk: Rules for AI agents in banking are still unsettled.

items.caption: The justices declined to hear the case, leaving a ruling that Fed banks can reject even eligible applicants. It's a setback for crypto banks seeking direct Fed access.
detail: The Supreme Court on Monday denied Custodia Bank's petition, leaving in place a Tenth Circuit ruling that Federal Reserve banks have discretion to reject master account applications, even from legally eligible banks.
Custodia, a Wyoming-chartered crypto bank, applied in October 2020 and was denied in January 2023. Lower courts sided with the Fed in 2024 and 2025.
A master account lets a bank plug straight into the Fed's payment system. Kraken got a limited master account in March 2026.

Big swings before one company's earnings are a reminder to check how much of your portfolio rides on a few tech names.
If you buy on a schedule, dips like this let the same dollars buy more shares.

items.headline: L3Harris falls 4% after Duffy ties it to the FAA outage; airlines face a ~$345M hit
items.caption: L3Harris shares slid after the Transportation Secretary questioned its air traffic work. Bernstein says the ground stop could cost the top four airlines about $345 million.
detail: L3Harris fell about 4% before the bell Monday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the company may have installed a defective router or was not doing good work. Early findings point to a router that flooded the network with connection attempts.
L3Harris says it is cooperating with the FAA probe. It has not accepted blame or said what the cost might be. Findings are still preliminary.

Bernstein estimates a combined pretax hit of about $345 million for American, Delta, United and Southwest, with a range of $270 million to $430 million. JetBlue canceled 28% of its Sunday schedule and American 22%, per BofA.
money: If your flight was canceled, ask the airline for a refund in cash, not just a voucher, if you chose not to travel.
Check whether your credit card's travel coverage pays for hotels or meals from the delays.
Investors in airline or defense stocks: one-off disruptions can hit a quarter's profit without changing the long-term picture.
risk: If a probe finds L3Harris at fault, it could face penalties or lose contract work.

sources.t: L3Harris Shares Fall 4% After US Transportation Secretary Links Contractor to Nationwide Aviation Disruption
Top four US airlines face $345 million hit from FAA ground stop, Bernstein estimates

items.headline: Quebecor goes public with a $31B bid for Telus; Telus board flags big regulatory risks
items.caption: Quebecor made an unsolicited merger offer for Telus valued at about $31 billion. Telus says it's reviewing it but sees serious approval risks.
detail: Quebecor sent an unsolicited offer to merge with Telus, valued at about $31 billion. It is an enhanced version of a private proposal from June.

Telus confirmed the offer Monday and said a special committee is reviewing it. Board chair John Manley said Quebecor still hasn't explained how the deal could pass Canada's telecom rules, and that a review would be long and costly.
Telus says it will also look at other options to maximize value. Quebecor says it went public because the deal affects consumers and shareholders.
money: Takeover fights can lift a target's stock, but the price can fall back fast if the bid fails.
Fewer big phone carriers can mean less price competition, so watch your wireless bill if consolidation happens.
If you own Telus, a board review often leads to a higher offer or a rival bid, but not always.
risk: Regulators could block the deal, and the offer could be withdrawn.

sources.t: Telus conducting 'thorough review' of $31B takeover offer from Québecor

items.headline: Kuo: OpenAI and Anthropic could take about 26 million Google TPUs in 2028-29
items.caption: Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo says new orders push Google's AI chip visibility out to 2029. Nvidia's mostly runs through 2027-early 2028, he says.
detail: Ming-Chi Kuo wrote Sunday that new OpenAI and Anthropic orders extend Google TPU shipment visibility to 2029. He estimates OpenAI seeks about 12 million TPUs and Anthropic about 14 million across 2028 and 2029.
Kuo says Nvidia GPUs and other AI chips mostly have visibility through late 2027 to mid-2028. He says uncertainty over Nvidia's CEO succession gives Google an opening with customers.
Nvidia stock fell 12.8% last week, its worst week since March 2025.
money: AI chip demand is spreading beyond Nvidia; broad tech funds catch more of that than single-stock bets.
Analyst estimates aren't orders. Treat them as one input, not a reason to trade.
If you hold Alphabet or Nvidia, know how much of your portfolio they make up before Tuesday's earnings.
risk: These are one analyst's estimates, not confirmed contracts.

items.headline: Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max at $1.50 per million input tokens, undercutting US rivals
items.caption: Alibaba's new flagship AI model costs far less than top US models. It claims a 62% cut in cost per task versus its last model.
detail: Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter model with a 1-million-token context window. It costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens on its API.

Alibaba says average cost per task on its own benchmark fell 62% from its previous model. Digital Trends notes Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4 in and $20 out, and Gemini 4 prices are set to double Dec. 1.
Smaller open-source Qwen4 models are expected later. Alibaba's safety claims haven't been tested by an outside red team yet.
money: If your business pays for AI by the token, price competition is a reason to compare providers every few months.
Gemini users: budget for the Dec. 1 price increase now.
Cheaper models can make AI tools affordable for side gigs and small businesses.
risk: Benchmarks and savings figures come from Alibaba itself.

detail: Zelle, run by bank group Early Warning Services, said at Breakpoint 2026 it will launch ZelleUSD (ZLUSD) on Solana for international person-to-person payments. The banks behind it include JPMorgan and Wells Fargo.
India is the first remittance corridor. Earlier plans said it would be live by the end of 2026, but no launch date was given on stage.
Zelle and Solana will also test privacy features that hide transfers from the public chain while letting banks check them for compliance.
money: Sending money abroad often costs several percent in fees; a bank-backed stablecoin route could cut that.
Until it launches, compare remittance fees and exchange rates before each transfer.
Stablecoins are only as safe as their issuer; stick with regulated, bank-backed options.
risk: No launch date yet, and fees haven't been announced.

Selling at a loss in a taxable account can offset gains elsewhere on your 2026 taxes.
Avoid leverage in a falling market; liquidations can wipe out positions fast.

items.headline: EU sanctions nearly 50 Russian banks and refinery operators; sends Ukraine ~$8.7B
items.caption: EU ministers listed 101 entities and 12 people tied to Russia's war funding. The bloc also approved its biggest single payment to Ukraine.
detail: EU foreign ministers sanctioned 12 people and 101 entities. The list includes nearly 50 Russian banks and financial firms, refinery operators and the St. Petersburg oil terminal.
Buyers of Russian oil products in the UAE, China, Seychelles and Oman were also listed, along with owners of sanctioned shadow-fleet ships. Owners tied to Wildberries and Ozon were named too.

The EU approved about $8.7 billion for Ukraine, its largest single payment, and Kyiv got $1.88 billion for drones and air defense. US-mediated talks in the UAE produced a prisoner swap but no breakthrough.
money: Tighter sanctions on Russian refining can keep diesel and fuel prices firm; budget for higher heating and trucking costs.
Energy stocks tend to react to sanction news; broad funds smooth that out.
Defense makers may benefit from steady European aid spending.
risk: Sanctions can be dodged through third countries, limiting their effect.

detail: Trump departed Monday on his first overseas trip since the midterms. He arrives in Manila Tuesday for Quad talks and is expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.

On Wednesday he meets Philippine President Marcos, then flies to Shenzhen for APEC. He meets Xi Jinping Thursday, followed by a first-ever meeting with Xi and Putin. Officials don't expect a concrete deal.
Elon Musk will join parts of the China travel. Trump and Xi plan to focus on carrying out their existing trade agreement.
money: Trade headlines can move stocks with big China exposure; avoid chasing moves on rumors.
Tariff changes eventually show up in prices of imported goods, so big purchases may be worth timing around clear news.
Farm, chip and auto stocks are the most sensitive to US-China outcomes.
risk: Talks could stall, and tariff threats elsewhere (like Mexico) add uncertainty.

items.caption: The Senate takes a key vote on an energy permitting overhaul Monday evening. Lawmakers have four weeks left to avoid a shutdown.
detail: The Senate's bipartisan energy permitting overhaul faces a vote Monday evening to limit debate on its latest version. Several judicial nominees are also lined up.
Government funding expires Dec. 11. Democrats say they'll back a spending bill only if it cuts off defense funds for the Iran war, which Republicans oppose.
The administration wants $50 billion for air traffic control after Friday's ground stop. Some Republicans also want a last party-line bill, with Trump seeking $350 billion for defense in it.
money: Federal workers and contractors: build a cash cushion now in case of a December shutdown.
Faster permitting could speed power and transmission projects, which matters for future electric bills.
If you rely on a federal service, get paperwork done before Dec. 11.
risk: A shutdown could delay some federal services and paychecks.

items.headline: New England governors ask Congress for $3B more in heating aid as oil prices jump
items.caption: Six governors want LIHEAP raised to $7 billion. They warn heating oil could cost about 50% more this winter.

visual.title: Winter heating squeeze
visual.label: Extra LIHEAP money six governors requested

detail: Governors of all six New England states, from both parties, asked appropriators for $3 billion more for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program. That would bring it to $7 billion.

They cite estimates that heating oil could rise about 50% this winter, adding about $1.1 billion in costs for low-income Northeast households. Massachusetts heating oil averaged $5.94 a gallon, over $2 more than a year earlier.
Massachusetts' LIHEAP allocation this year is $142.3 million, down from last year after extra infrastructure-law money ran out. Only about 20% of eligible households get help each year.
money: Apply for LIHEAP early; many states pay on a first-come basis until funds run out.
Ask your utility about budget billing to spread winter costs evenly.
Weatherizing drafts and lowering the thermostat a few degrees can trim a heating bill noticeably.
risk: Congress may not approve extra money before cold weather hits.

items.headline: Medicare extends its freeze on new home health and hospice providers through May 2027
items.caption: CMS kept a nationwide pause on new home health and hospice enrollments for six more months, citing fraud. Existing providers can now add locations.

visual.title: What the freeze means
items: New home health agencies and hospices can't enroll in Medicare
Runs six more months, through May 12, 2027

Current patients and services are not affected

detail: CMS extended its nationwide moratorium on new Medicare home health and hospice enrollments by six months. The freeze first started May 13, 2026.
Administrator Mehmet Oz said fraud in these areas persists. The pause blocks new agencies and some ownership changes that need new enrollment.
Unlike before, enrolled providers can now add practice locations. Critics say the freeze has delayed expansions and hurt access in underserved areas.
money: If you or a parent uses home health or hospice, current Medicare coverage continues as before.
Check that any provider you choose is already Medicare-enrolled to avoid surprise bills.
Report suspicious billing on your Medicare Summary Notice; fraud raises costs for everyone.
risk: Fewer new providers could mean longer waits in some areas.

items.headline: IRS shuts its old FIRE e-filing system for 1099s on Nov. 19; businesses move to IRIS
items.caption: Businesses still filing information returns through FIRE must finish by 3 p.m. ET Thursday. The replacement, IRIS, opens in January 2027.
detail: The IRS set Nov. 19, 2026 at 3 p.m. Eastern as the final cutoff for electronic filing through FIRE, its system for information returns like 1099s.
IRIS replaces it starting January 2027. FIRE credentials won't work in IRIS, so filers need a new IRIS TCC, and IRIS doesn't take FIRE-style .dat files.
Some foreign filers can use a separate system called IDES.
money: Small businesses: apply for an IRIS TCC now so January 1099 filing isn't delayed.
Late or missing 1099s can bring IRS penalties; plan the switch early.
If you use a payroll or tax software provider, confirm it will file through IRIS for you.
risk: Filers who wait may hit setup delays during the busy January season.

Small, cash-burning companies can need to raise money, which can dilute existing shareholders.

With the 10-year yield above 5%, Treasuries offer a real alternative to stocks for cautious money.
Spreading money across sectors lowers the damage when one hot area cools.

items.headline: Health care deal Monday: Lilly buys Calytrix for up to $1.5B; Medtronic adds Contego
items.caption: Eli Lilly agreed to buy blood cancer biotech Calytrix Bio for up to $1.5 billion. Medtronic plans to buy Contego Medical, valued at $380 million.
detail: Eli Lilly is buying Calytrix Bio, a Massachusetts startup working on an antibody for two rare blood cancers, myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia. The deal is worth up to $1.5 billion, but the guaranteed cash portion wasn't disclosed. It extends Lilly's recent buying streak.

Medtronic plans to buy Contego Medical, which makes carotid artery and clot-removal devices. Medtronic already distributed Contego's products in the US. It expects a small hit to adjusted earnings per share in fiscal 2027 and 2028, then a neutral or positive effect.
money: 'Up to' deal prices include milestone payments that may never be paid, so the real cost is often lower.
Drug giants with big cash flow keep buying startups; health care funds give broad exposure without picking winners.
Small earnings dilution from deals is normal; watch whether the buyer delivers the promised growth later.
risk: Early-stage drugs often fail in trials.

If you're buying the game, compare console bundles and retailer deals before launch day.
Gaming stocks swing on single titles, so a broad fund spreads that hit-or-miss risk.
risk: Delays or weak early sales could hit the stock hard.

Airlines and truckers gain when fuel falls; energy producers lose.
risk: A confirmed attack could send prices jumping fast.

items.headline: 2027 standard deduction rises to $33,200 for couples; 65+ extra goes to $2,100
items.caption: The standard deduction climbs $1,000 for married couples and $500 for singles in 2027. Older filers get a slightly bigger extra amount.
detail: Inflation adjustments lift the 2027 standard deduction to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, $16,600 for singles and $24,950 for heads of household. These apply to returns filed in 2028.

People 65 and older get an extra amount on top: $2,100 for single or head-of-household filers and $1,700 per qualifying spouse for married filers. Blind filers get double. The separate $6,000 senior deduction still runs through 2028 and phases out above $75,000 of income for singles and $150,000 for couples.
money: Most people take the standard deduction; a higher one quietly lowers taxable income without extra work.
If your itemized deductions are close to the new amounts, 'bunching' gifts or payments into one year may help.
Seniors can stack the age-based extra with the $6,000 senior deduction if income qualifies.
risk: The $6,000 senior deduction phases out at higher incomes.

sources.t: IRS Updates Tax Deduction for People Age 65 and Older

items.headline: IRS sees more complaints about tax preparers misusing AI; new guidance coming
items.caption: The IRS office that disciplines tax pros says AI-related referrals are starting to rise. It plans more guidance within a couple of months.

visual.title: IRS Office of Professional Responsibility
visual.label: Cases involving AI, out of about 200 open.

detail: The IRS Office of Professional Responsibility, which oversees tax practitioner conduct, has fewer than five AI-related cases among about 200. Director Thomas Curtin says such referrals are starting to tick up.
The office issued an alert in June applying its practitioner rules, called Circular 230, to AI use. Curtin said more guidance is coming in the next couple of months. The office has just 15 staff.
money: Ask your preparer how they use AI and who reviews the final return; you're responsible for what's filed.
Double-check AI-generated tax advice against IRS publications before acting on it.
A credentialed preparer (CPA, EA or attorney) is bound by IRS conduct rules, which gives you recourse.
risk: Errors on your return can bring penalties even if a tool made them.

items.headline: Judge bars ICE from reading an immigration lawyer's seized phone data for now
items.caption: A federal judge in Boston found the lawyer is likely to prove his phone was seized in retaliation for his speech. The government says it was part of an investigation.

visual.title: Lattarulo v. government
items: Phone seized at Boston Logan without a warrant
Data copied; phone returned 8 days later
Data must stay unreadable while the case goes on
Government cites a probe of his firm's hiring

detail: US District Judge Allison Burroughs granted a preliminary injunction for Andrew Lattarulo, part owner of an immigration law firm. Agents took his phone at Boston Logan Airport in September as he returned from Aruba, copied its data and returned it eight days later. He runs a popular Instagram account with know-your-rights videos.

The judge found he would likely show the search was retaliation for protected speech, and ordered the data kept unreadable until the case ends. She did not order it destroyed or rule on the Fourth Amendment. The government denies targeting his speech and says the search was tied to an inquiry into whether his firm employed unauthorized workers.
money: Border searches of phones are legal in many cases; travelers can limit what's stored on devices they carry.
Businesses should keep work-authorization (I-9) records complete, since hiring probes can be costly.
Legal fights like this can raise costs for small law firms; budgeting for compliance helps.
risk: This is an early ruling; the case continues.

items.headline: Texas bill would send $1,500 relief checks to every adult, paid from the rainy day fund
items.caption: State Sen. Roland Gutierrez filed SB 297, a $17 billion plan for one-time checks. It faces likely opposition in the Republican-led Senate.

visual.title: Texas SB 297
visual.label: One-time check proposed for adult Texans.

detail: Democratic State Sen. Roland Gutierrez of San Antonio filed Senate Bill 297. It would send $1,500 emergency relief checks to Texans 18 and older who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2027. People would apply online or by mail, and most checks would go out by the end of 2027.

The $17 billion cost would come from the state's roughly $27 billion rainy day fund, which needs legislative approval to tap. The bill argues an affordability crisis counts as a public calamity, the exception that allows direct payments. Democrats now control the Texas House, but the Republican Senate is likely to resist.

items.headline: Retirees: take your 2026 required IRA withdrawal by Dec. 31 or risk a 25% penalty

detail: Required minimum distributions (RMDs) are yearly withdrawals the IRS makes you take from tax-deferred retirement accounts. If you will be 74 or older by the end of 2026, your 2026 RMD is due by Dec. 31.

If you turn 73 this year, your first RMD can wait until April 1, 2027. Roth IRAs don't require them, and you can skip your current job's 401(k) if you still work there and own under 5% of the company.
To figure it, divide your Dec. 31, 2025 balance by the IRS life-expectancy factor. At 75 that factor is 24.6, so a $100,000 IRA needs about $4,065 out. Missing it can cost a 25% penalty.
money: Subtract anything you already withdrew this year; you only need to take the rest.

items.headline: Oregon property taxes are due today: pay in full to get a 3% discount
items.caption: Because Nov. 15 fell on a Sunday, Oregon's first property tax payment is due Monday. Paying the full year now earns a 3% discount.

items.t: Last day to appeal your value

detail: Oregon property tax bills are normally due Nov. 15. This year that was a Sunday, so the deadline moves to Monday, Nov. 16.

Pay the whole bill by the deadline and you get a 3% discount. Pay two-thirds and you get 2%. Pay at least one-third to stay current, with the rest due Feb. 15 and May 17. Mailed payments must be postmarked by the due date.
Watch fees. In Multnomah County, eChecks cost $1.50, debit cards $3.95 and credit cards 2.55%. Owners there can appeal their assessed value through Dec. 31.
money: On a $4,000 bill, paying in full saves $120. That beats most savings accounts for the same cash.
Use eCheck, not a credit card. A 2.55% card fee eats most of the 3% discount.
If your value looks too high, file an appeal by Dec. 31. A lower value cuts future bills too.
risk: Bank bill-pay counts when funds arrive, so a same-day send may be late.
Don't drain your emergency fund to grab the discount.

items.headline: Family of a Houston man hit by an ICE vehicle says it was intentional
items.caption: A Texas grand jury indicted the ICE officer on aggravated assault. ICE says the man ran in front of the vehicle and calls the prosecution a political stunt.

items.t: Lawmakers write to ICE and DHS

detail: Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, a construction worker who has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, was struck by an ICE vehicle in Houston on Oct. 10. Video shows him running before the vehicle hits him from behind. He was not the target of the operation and remains in ICE custody.

A Harris County grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales on a felony aggravated assault charge. The officer's lawyer calls it an accident. ICE says Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle and calls the case a political stunt.

ICE does not dispute that he has no criminal record but says he is in the country illegally. His siblings told CBS News the act was intentional. House Democrats led by Rep. Lizzie Fletcher accused ICE of limiting family and lawyer access.
money: Detention can wipe out a household's income overnight. Families should know where key papers and bank access are kept.
Construction and other labor-heavy fields may face worker shortages and higher costs as enforcement continues.
For immigration questions, a licensed attorney or accredited representative is worth the cost over a notario.
risk: The criminal case is in early stages; facts are disputed.
Outcomes may shape how state prosecutors handle federal agents.

detail: Plainclothes ICE agents detained Agustin Baccega and Gustavo Romanello, a married couple who work as acrobats, at Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport last weekend. They came to the U.S. on visas in 2020 and soon applied for asylum. Those cases are still pending.

ICE called it a targeted action and said both overstayed their visas. A spokesperson said a pending application or work permit does not give legal status. ICE would not say how agents knew the men would be there.

Their Phoenix lawyer, in practice 17 years, says arrests of people with similar profiles and at airports have risen sharply this year. The airport says it is not told about federal enforcement and doesn't get passenger data.

Detention can halt a paycheck fast. Keep an emergency fund and give a trusted person access if you can.

detail: Summit Therapeutics said Sunday the FDA sent a Complete Response Letter, meaning its application for ivonescimab can't be approved as filed. The drug was meant for advanced EGFR-mutated lung cancer after earlier targeted treatment.

The FDA said a progression-free survival gain alone was not enough without a statistically significant overall survival benefit. Summit's HARMONi trial hit its PFS goal but its survival result only trended positive. Summit says it will keep running other late-stage trials.
On the flip side, Helus Pharma rose more than 23% overnight before topline Phase 3 results for its depression drug HLP003, set for Monday.

items.headline: Supreme Court takes a Robinhood IPO case that could reshape investor lawsuits
items.caption: Justices will decide if a company can be sued for leaving out interim numbers without a misleading statement. Robinhood's 2021 IPO is the test case.
detail: The Supreme Court agreed Friday to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha. Investors sued because Robinhood's July 2021 IPO did not include some interim financial data that wasn't due until August 2021.

The question is whether a company can be liable for omitting material interim information without also showing the omission made another statement misleading. The Ninth Circuit ruled against Robinhood, and the federal government sided with Robinhood on taking the case.
SCOTUSblog expects arguments in spring 2027.
money: A pro-company ruling could make it harder for IPO buyers to recover losses in class actions; weigh new-issue risk accordingly.
Read the 'recent developments' section of any IPO prospectus, like Anthropic's this week.
If you're in a securities class action, track this case before settling expectations on payouts.
